title: Comparative analysis of loan risk forecasting using quantum machine learning and classical machine learning models
abstract_summary: This preprint compares classical SVM and a quantum-enhanced QSVM for loan default prediction on a Kaggle credit-risk dataset (≈12.6k records, 12 features). The authors report that QSVM slightly outperforms SVM (TPR 93.2%, TNR 87.6%) with a reported AUC of 1.0, arguing that QSVM may scale better and offer improved accuracy for larger financial datasets.
methodology_description: The study performed a comparative, empirical evaluation of a classical Support Vector Machine (SVM) and a quantum-enhanced SVM (QSVM/QSVC) for loan default prediction. The authors used a publicly available Kaggle credit-risk dataset and executed the experiments in a Jupyter environment. Data preprocessing included mean imputation for numeric missing values, mode imputation for categorical missing values, label encoding of categorical variables, and Min-Max normalization (MinMaxScaler). The dataset (≈12.6k records, 12 features) was split 80% train / 20% test. The classical model used an RBF kernel SVM (regularization C set to 10). The quantum model used a quantum-kernelized SVM implemented with Qiskit: classical inputs were embedded via a ZFeatureMap with two repetitions, mapped onto 12 qubits (one qubit per feature), and a quantum kernel (based on the ZFeatureMap) was computed on a statevector_simulator quantum instance (noise-free). Both models were evaluated using confusion matrices, precision, recall, F1-score, accuracy, ROC curves and AUC; learning curves (training vs cross-validation accuracy versus training set size) were also produced to study generalization as sample size increased.

Train/test split 80/20; learning curves computed with cross-validation.

Reported size ~12,638 rows and 12 features including age, income, employment length, loan amount, interest rate, loan percent of income, loan history length, home, intent, grade, employee length, and binary loan status (default indicator).

key_findings: [supported] On a Kaggle credit-risk dataset of ~12,638 records and 12 features, the authors ran comparative experiments between a classical SVM and a Quantum SVM (QSVM) implemented with a quantum kernel (QSVC) in Qiskit.
[supported] Both SVM and QSVM achieved the same overall test accuracy of 0.90 on the reported test set.
[supported] QSVM achieved a higher true positive rate (reported 93.2%) and higher true negative rate (reported 87.6%) than the SVM (reported TP ~92.5%, TN ~87.x), as reported by the authors.
[supported] QSVM is reported to have achieved an AUC of 1.0 (perfect ROC), whereas the classical SVM achieved an AUC of 0.898.
[supported] QSVM correctly predicted 1,186 of 1,272 actual default loans (authors' reported counts) and missed 156 'safe' loans (authors' reported count).
[supported] Experimental QSVM setup: 12 qubits, ZFeatureMap with two repetitions, regularization C=10, quantum backend = statevector_simulator (noise-free simulator), quantum kernel / QSVC used.

[supported] Data preprocessing steps used by the authors: mean imputation for numeric missing values, mode imputation for categorical, label encoding for categoricals, and Min–Max scaling for features.

[supported] Learning-curve behavior reported: SVM training score plateaued ~0.89 and cross-validation ~0.855 (plateau around 8,000 samples); QSVM training started ~0.93 then leveled ~0.91 while cross-validation rose to ~0.90 as sample size increased.

results_summary: The preprint reports an experiment on a 12,638-record Kaggle credit-risk dataset comparing a classical SVM (RBF kernel) to a QSVM implemented as a QSVC with a quantum kernel (ZFeatureMap, two repetitions) run on a noise-free statevector simulator. Both models achieved the same overall accuracy (0.90) on the test set, but the authors report slightly better class-level performance for QSVM (TPR 93.2%, TNR 87.6% vs. SVM TPR ~92.5%, TNR ~87.x) and a claimed perfect ROC AUC of 1.0 for QSVM compared with 0.898 for SVM. The experiment used 12 qubits, C=10 regularization, and standard preprocessing (imputation, label encoding, Min–Max scaling). The authors interpret these results as evidence that QSVM can outperform classical SVM and may scale favorably with larger datasets, although those broader claims are speculative within the paper.

Experimental hyperparameters reported: 12 qubits, QSVC regularization C = 10, ZFeatureMap with 2 repetitions, backend = statevector_simulator.
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper empirically reports a modest quantum advantage on the tested dataset: QSVM shows marginally better class-level metrics (higher TPR/TNR) and a reported perfect AUC (1.0) compared with the classical SVM (AUC 0.898). However, the experiments were executed on a noise-free statevector simulator (not on noisy hardware), overall accuracy was identical (0.90) for both models, and the claim that advantage will extend to larger, real-world datasets and to hardware remains speculative. Thus the advantage is demonstrated within the narrow, simulated experiment but its generality and practical significance are unproven.

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — The QSVM (quantum-kernel SVM) is reported to slightly outperform the classical RBF SVM on the Kaggle credit-risk dataset (reported QSVM TPR 93.2%, TNR 87.6%, AUC=1.0 vs SVM AUC=0.898).
#idea:hybrid-approach — The study uses a hybrid pipeline: classical preprocessing and an SVM classifier combined with a quantum kernel computed via Qiskit (ZFeatureMap) on a statevector simulator.
#limitation:simulation-only — All quantum-kernel evaluations were performed on a noise-free statevector_simulator; no experiments on real QPUs or with realistic noise models were reported.
#limitation:no-empirical-validation — The absence of real-hardware runs and lack of noise modelling limit claims about practical, near-term performance.
#limitation:data-encoding — Authors map 12 classical features to 12 qubits using a ZFeatureMap (1 qubit per feature); the cost and scalability of this encoding are not analysed.
#limitation:qubit-count — The experiments use only 12 qubits (one per feature), a small-scale demonstration that does not establish performance on higher-dimensional or production credit datasets.

#contradiction:classical-vs-quantum — Despite claiming quantum superiority, overall accuracy is identical (0.90) for both models and most class-level metrics are very similar, calling the practical significance of the claimed advantage into question.

#contradiction:scalability — The paper asserts potential better scaling of QSVM to larger datasets, but provides no larger-scale experiments or hardware results and uses a noise-free simulator, which contradicts the scalability claim.
contradictions: The paper claims a clear quantum advantage (AUC=1.0 for QSVM) while reporting identical overall accuracy (0.90) and very similar precision/recall/F1 to the classical SVM — this suggests the advantage is marginal or possibly an artifact (overfitting, metric/reporting error).

Authors argue QSVM will scale better to larger financial datasets, but experiments are limited to a 12-feature, ~12.6k-row dataset encoded with one qubit per feature and run on a noise-free statevector simulator; this contradicts the scaling claim in the absence of noisy/hardware experiments or larger benchmarks.
Use of a statevector (noise-free) simulator and absence of any noise model or QPU runs contradict practical claims about near-term feasibility — results may not translate to realistic noisy hardware.
No comprehensive hyperparameter search, unspecified random seed and lack of shared code/notebook raise reproducibility concerns that undermine the strength of the reported comparative results.
